series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/7] NFSD: validate transport name in listener_set before serv creation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a validation check in the NFS daemon to ensure that the transport name specified by the user is one of the supported protocols (tcp, udp, or rdma) before creating a new service. This prevents an arbitrary string from being passed to the svc_xprt_create_from_sa function, which can trigger a request_module upcall under nfsd_mutex. The validation check is done in the nfsd_nl_validate_listeners function, which runs before nfsd_mutex is taken.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/7] NFSD: cap the number of listeners accepted in listener_set
series_items.patch_summary: This patch limits the number of listeners accepted in a single request to NFSD_NL_LISTENER_MAX (1024) to prevent long spin times in atomic context due to nested loops. The existing limit was not capped, allowing for up to ~1M iterations under sv_lock. The new limit is far above any realistic configuration and only rejects requests with an excessively large listener list.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/7] SUNRPC: keep the first error in svc_register()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the svc_register() function in the SUNRPC module to keep track of the first error encountered during RPC program registration, rather than overwriting it with subsequent errors. This change is necessary because the current behavior can lead to unexpected results when registering multiple programs, particularly in cases where some programs fail to register but others succeed. The patch ensures that only the first error is returned, which helps to prevent issues such as a server failing to bring up any listeners due to a partial failure during registration.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/7] SUNRPC: bound the local rpcbind client timeout to 1s
series_items.patch_summary: This patch limits the timeout for the local rpcbind client to 1 second. The previous default timeouts of 10 seconds for AF_LOCAL and 60 seconds for loopback TCP fallback were causing stalls in NFS server operations, leading to hung-task watchdog warnings. By reducing the timeout, the patch shortens the stall time but does not completely eliminate it. The real fix would be to make the registration asynchronous, which is a more complex task.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/7] NFSD: report listener creation failures through extack
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves error reporting for NFS listener creation failures by providing a detailed message through the extack mechanism, including the transport and error code. This allows userland to better diagnose issues such as an unreachable local rpcbind. The patch only affects the handling of LISTENER_SET errors and leaves other rejection cases unchanged.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 6/7] selftests/nfsd: exercise listener_set request validation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new self-test to the NFS daemon (NFSD) that exercises listener_set request validation. The test checks various invalid and valid scenarios, including bad or absent transport names, missing addresses, truncated or unsupported socket addresses, and malformed entries. It also tests LISTENER_GET against an empty net namespace. The test uses kselftest_harness.h to run in its own network namespace and masks /run to prevent interference with the host's rpcbind registration. The patch includes a new Makefile target for NFSD and config options to enable NFS and IPv6 support.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 7/7] selftests/nfsd: add a per-netns rpcbind stub and the listener round-trips
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a per-network namespace (netns) rpcbind stub to the selftests/nfsd suite, allowing tests to run within their own netns without relying on the host's rpcbind service. The stub is implemented as a minimal responder that binds to a local socket and responds to RPCBVERS_2 and RPCBVERS_4 requests. The patch also includes new test cases for listener registration and round-trips over TCP, UDP, and IPv6 connections, including edge cases such as empty-list serv destroy and -EBUSY refusal.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch set hardens the netlink listener interfaces in the NFS daemon (nfsd) and SunRPC code to prevent stalls under nfsd_mutex. The changes include rejecting invalid transport names, capping the number of listeners accepted in a request, keeping the first error in svc_register(), bounding the local rpcbind client timeout, reporting listener creation failures through extack, and adding validation tests for listener_set requests. Additionally, per-netns rpcbind stubs are added and listener round-trip tests are implemented to improve performance and prevent hangs.

patches_submitted.subject: memcg stats flushing (WAS "Re: [PATCH] fuse: disable default bdi strictlimiting")

version_history.subject: memcg stats flushing (WAS "Re: [PATCH] fuse: disable default bdi strictlimiting")

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses the issue of stale memory cgroup (memcg) stats causing premature OOM kills by proposing a solution to reduce the overhead of updating and flushing these statistics. The idea is for memcg to accumulate updates on a per-CPU basis, then propagate them up to a global atomic counter when it reaches a certain threshold, eliminating the need for frequent flushing. This approach aims to scale better for large machines with many cores and focuses on reducing the number of stats that require flushing, specifically NR_FILE_DIRTY and NR_WRITEBACK in the writeback case.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledges that the flush operation would need to touch multiple cachelines per CPU on a large machine, but does not provide a clear resolution or plan for addressing this issue.
review_comments.raw_body:
Sorry, I think I messed up how things got linked when trying to update
the thread title in gmail. This is a continuation of the previous
discussion thread ("PATCH] fuse: disable default bdi strictlimiting")
which is at https://lore.kernel.org/linux-fsdevel/s4kv7qep3jlncs67q72xfhserpd66hpbwzkoppiddc5raufyjd@ksuvlfqcrbk2/T/#t.

Thanks,
Joanne

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Yosry Ahmed noted that the patch may not address premature OOM kills due to stale stats in the vmscan path, citing a test where VMs experienced OOM kills after the ratelimited flush, and suggested further investigation is needed.

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed questioned the trade-off between update and read performance in memcg stats, suggesting that increasing the cost of updates could improve the manageability of the read path, which is becoming slow in some cases.

The reviewer pointed out that memcg stats perform similar per-CPU counting and thresholding as vmstat, but with a cgroup hierarchy, which requires reading hierarchical stats including children. They suggested replacing the current flushing logic with updating the stat on each parent or forgoing the rstat flushing logic altogether.

Reviewer suggested side-stepping the flushing issue by either keeping track of CPUs with updates via rstat or propagating per-CPU stat updates when reaching a threshold, similar to how vmstat handles batching
review_comments.raw_body:
I don't think we had time to look into this closely. We have a test
that runs VMs with some memory pressure / reclaim, and we observed OOM
kills in that test after the ratelimited flush in the vmscan path.
Whether or not this translates to additional OOM kills in our prod is
currently unknown, but it's a signal that reclaim effectiveness may be
negatively affected in some cases.

---

Yeah I think we generally want to keep updates faster than reads,
because some of them are also in latency-sensitive paths like
networking. However, since reads are becoming too slow in some cases,
the question here is whether we can afford some extra cost on the
update side (to iterate parent per-CPU counters) to make the read path
more manageable.

---

The memcg stats perform similar per-CPU counting and thresholding. The
main difference from vmstat AFAICT is the cgroup hierarchy. In vmstat
we have per-CPU counters and a global atomic counter for each stat.
For memcg, we have the same for each cgroup, then we also have a
cgroup tree. When we read the stats of a cgroup, we usually want the
hierarchical stats including all of its children, so we can't just
read the global counter.

We use rstat, a cgroup framework that keeps track of which cgroups
have updates on which CPUs, and then memcg has thresholding logic on
top to only flush if the number of pending updates exceeds a
threshold. Essentially, if the magnitude updates on a CPU exceeds
MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH, we add it to a global per-memcg counter. We only
flush if that global per-memcg counter has > NR_CPUS *
MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH updates. So in theory I think we tolerate up to 2 *
NR_CPUS * MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH of stale stats (combined for all the
stats).

See memcg_rstat_updated() and memcg_vmstats_needs_flush() for this logic.

Looking at this code again, it made me realize that we already iterate
the per-CPU stats_updates on every update to increment the number of
pending stats on this CPU. I wonder if we can replace this with
actually updating the stat on each parent, then the flush path only
needs to accumulate CPU counters. Or maybe as you mention, we update
the global per-memcg counter when updates on a CPU exceed a threshold,
and forgo the rstat flushing logic completely.

---

Probably not (hence I called it radical), but I think this can be
side-stepped by either keeping the tracking of CPUs that have updates
via rstat (or similar), or just propagating the per-CPU stat updates
when they reach a threshold like vmstat.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing concerns about the performance impact of flushing memcg stats and exploring an alternative approach to batching updates. She proposes running experiments to test updating global per-memcg counters in batches, but notes that this may incur a nontrivial performance hit due to unconditional walking of ancestors on every update.
review_comments.raw_body:
I can run some experiments and see if updating the global per-memcg
counter per batch and forgoing flushing could be a viable solution. I
can use my setup to test it for writeback, but for the zswap use case,
what's the best way to test if the changes are too expensive? Is there
a benchmark program you're running?

For updating the stat on each parent and having the flush path only
accumulate CPU counters, I think this means we would have to
unconditionally walk the ancestors + update its counters on every
update, as we wouldn't be able to early break if the flushable
threshold was already exceeded. I don't think we could replace the
stats_update update, as it seems like readers still need some way of
knowing when to flush. It seems like this could be a nontrivial
performance hit, but maybe it's a non-factor in reality. If you think
this would be useful to get benchmark numbers on, I can run some
experiments on this too.

Thanks,
Joanne

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer suggested that memcg could use a batching approach similar to vmstat, where the per-CPU counter is accumulated and propagated up to a global atomic counter only when it reaches a threshold, potentially eliminating the need for flushing.

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed suggested experimenting with shifting workload between update and reader sides for memcg stats flushing, proposing two options: (a) updating per-CPU counters directly on stats updates or (b) using a global atomic counter that's updated when the per-CPU threshold is exceeded. He also proposed running benchmarks to test worst-case scenarios.
review_comments.raw_body:
I was running stress-ng and measuring the latency of zswap_load() and
zswap_store() with bpftrace. But I suspect whatever works for writeback
should work for zswap :)

---

I think we need to experiment with how much work we can shift around
between the update and reader sides.

Right now, on the update side, we call __css_rstat_updated(), which
iterates the parents and puts them on the per-CPU rstat tree, then we
iterate the parents again in memcg_rstat_updated() and:
- Check if flushing threshold is already met.
- Update per-CPU counter for stats_updates.
- If per-CPU update exceeds (another) threshold, we update an atomic for
  stats_updates.

The flush side checks the flushing threshold and does an rstat flush,
which will walk the update trees on all CPUs and iterates all child
cgroups on it. Pretty expensive when the threshold is met.

I think we discussed two different options:

(a) On stats updates, iterate the parents and update the per-CPU
counters of the stat directly.

In this case, we can't keep using rstat, as we would still need to add
the cgroup and all its ancestors to the update tree anyway and the flush
cost will remain similar. So on the flush path we'll need to iterate all
CPUs and add the counters. We can explore if use a cpumask can help
here, but perhaps not since we'll need to update it atomically on all
stat updates.

I imagine that if we do this we'll drop the stats_updates optimization
to avoid adding more cost to the update side. We'll be replacing parent
stats_updates modification with parent stat counter modification. But
maybe it's feasible to keep both to limit the cost of flusing.

This only works if the cost of iterate the CPUs on the flush side ends
up being cheaper than the current flush. I imagine the average cost will
be higher but the cost should be much more consistent vs the current
flush, so the tail should be better.

(b) On stats updates, iterate the parents and update the per-CPU
counters of the stat directly AND update a global atomic if the per-CPU
counter exceeds a threshold. I think updates may get too expensive as we
may need to update multiple atomics, especially when updating the root
counter as it will be contended by all cgroups.

The flush side becomes an atomic read, so should be very cheap, and we
can drop other heuristics and optimizations.

---

I think ultimately we need to experiment with these approachs (and
perhaps others) to check what actually works in practice. You'll
probably want some benchmarks or synthetic tests with many cgroups to
exercise the worst case scenarios.

For the zswap stats, I used to run stress-ng with a bunch of workers
(20, 50, 100, ..) in cgroups of different levels. Since all workers are
in the same cgroups, all the parents are common and all threads end up
competing on the same atomics, so worst case scenario. I was also
testing in a VM that has more CPUs than stress-ng workers, to exercise
the full extent of the concurrency and contention.

This could be a lot of work, so I am not really asking you to do it, but
just brainstorming and sharing ideas :)

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: memcg stats flushing (WAS "Re: [PATCH] fuse: disable default bdi strictlimiting")

patches_acked.patch_summary: Patch addresses a memory accounting issue in memcg-v1, specifically fixing the failcnt counter for memory.memsw.

review_comments.author: Johannes Weiner
review_comments.summary: Raised a valid point about kmem.tcp.limit_in_bytes being deprecated, suggested adding a conditional statement for track_failcnt.

review_comments.author: Guopeng Zhang
review_comments.summary: Agreed to add the requested conditional statement and update the changelog in a new version.
review_comments.raw_body:
\u5728 2026/8/11 03:09, Johannes Weiner \u5199\u9053:
> On Mon, Aug 10, 2026 at 03:42:47PM +0800, Guopeng Zhang wrote:
>> From: Guopeng Zhang <zhangguopeng@kylinos.cn>
>>
>> Commit 0e2759afcaf9 ("page_counter: track failcnt only for legacy
>> cgroups") made failcnt accounting conditional on track_failcnt. It
>> enabled the flag for memcg->memory, but not for memcg->memsw.
>>
>> Consequently, memory.memsw.failcnt remains zero when the memory+swap
>> limit is hit. Enable failcnt accounting for the v1 memsw counter.
>>
>> Reproducer:
>>
>>     CG=/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memsw-test
>>     LIMIT=33554432
>>     mkdir "$CG"
>>     echo "$LIMIT" > "$CG/memory.limit_in_bytes"
>>     echo "$LIMIT" > "$CG/memory.memsw.limit_in_bytes"
>>
>> Start a child process in the cgroup and make it allocate and touch 96 MiB
>> of memory, causing a memcg OOM.
>>
>>     cat "$CG/memory.memsw.failcnt"
>>
>> Without the patch, memory.memsw.failcnt is 0. With the patch,
>> memory.memsw.failcnt is greater than 0.
>>
>> Fixes: 0e2759afcaf9 ("page_counter: track failcnt only for legacy cgroups")

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2 00/17] selftests/mm: improve khugepaged coverage

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 01/17] selftests/mm: skip collapse_compound_extreme where the PMD is too large
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies a selftest to skip a test case where the PMD (Page Map Directory) size is too large, specifically larger than 32M. The test in question, collapse_compound_extreme, relies on being able to allocate multiple PMD-order allocations, which becomes unreliable for very large PMDs. By skipping this test case when the PMD size exceeds 32M, the patch prevents a failure that would cause the entire binary to stop running and lose subsequent test cases.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 02/17] selftests/mm: scale khugepaged's collapse wait with the PMD size
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adjusts the wait time for khugepaged's collapse operation to scale with the PMD size. The original three-second wait is kept as a floor, and an additional second is added per 128M of memory being collapsed. This change aims to prevent false timeouts in cases where the collapse takes longer due to larger PMDs, while still allowing real failures to be reported within a reasonable time frame.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 03/17] selftests/mm: skip khugepaged page cache cases without a PMD folio
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the selftests/mm/khugepaged test suite to skip certain cases related to khugepaged page cache when a PMD folio is not supported. The issue arises from a global cap on page cache order, which prevents PMD-sized page cache folios and causes the kernel to refuse collapses in these cases. The patch adds checks for this condition and skips shmem and file operations if a PMD-order page cache folio is not supported. If no operations are left to collapse into, the test suite exits with a skip message.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 04/17] selftests/mm: retry the swapout the khugepaged swap cases rely on
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged selftest to retry swapout operations when they fail due to a best-effort MADV_PAGEOUT call. The test will wait up to two seconds before reporting failure, allowing for occasional failures caused by folios still under writeback from an earlier pageout. This change is intended to improve the reliability of the khugepaged selftest on certain architectures, such as arm64 with 64K pages.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 05/17] selftests/mm: move is_backed_by_folio() into vm_util
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the is_backed_by_folio() function from split_huge_page_test.c to vm_util.c, making it available for use in other tests. The function checks if an address range is backed by a folio of a given order by reading the compound head and tail flags from /proc/kpageflags. This change allows for more reuse of code across different selftests and does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 06/17] selftests/mm: add folio-order check for address ranges
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function called `is_range_backed_by_folio_orders` to the Linux kernel's selftests/mm module. The function checks whether an address range is backed by folios of a specific order, and returns true if it is. This is useful for testing memory allocation and deallocation scenarios where folio ordering matters. The function works by checking each window of the address range to see if it maps exactly one folio of the specified order, with the first PFN being the folio head and the subsequent PFNs being contiguous. If any window fails this check, the function returns false.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 07/17] selftests/mm: add folio-order detection self-check
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a self-test to verify that the vm_util folio-order detection helpers agree with the kernel about what backs a mapping. The test faults in memory with only one order enabled and checks that the helpers report exactly that order, not a neighbouring order or plain 4K memory as order 0. This ensures that the helpers are reliable before they are used by khugepaged mTHP tests to detect collapse results.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 08/17] selftests/mm: add khugepaged completion barrier helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a helper function to the selftests/mm module that allows tests to drive the khugepaged daemon in a controlled manner. The helper, called thp_update_num(), writes sysfs knobs only when their values change, preventing unnecessary wake-ups of the daemon. This is necessary because settings pushes must not start scan passes without explicit permission from the caller. The patch also introduces a new function, khugepaged_full_pass(), which drives the daemon in step and waits for full scans to advance by two. This allows tests to check the result of a full scan pass.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 09/17] selftests/mm: add order-parameterized khugepaged collapse cases
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds four new test cases to the selftests/mm/khugepaged context, which checks how large pages are collapsed by the khugepaged mechanism. The new cases check each aligned window individually and verify that only the populated window collapses in certain scenarios. Each case faults its region before MADV_HUGEPAGE with only the target order enabled, so the sources are always order 0 and the collapse product can only come from khugepaged. This patch aims to improve the testing of khugepaged's behavior by adding more specific and detailed test cases.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 10/17] selftests/mm: parameterize the mixed-source collapse case by source order
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the selftests/mm/khugepaged.c test to parameterize the mixed-source collapse case by source order. The test faults a region as order-2 folios and collapses them to the target, but allows for other supported mTHP orders below the target when specified with the -s option. This change is intended to make the test more flexible and adaptable to different system configurations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 11/17] selftests/mm: cover a shared-source collapse write race
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test case to the selftests/mm/khugepaged.c file, which checks for a shared-source collapse write race in the Linux kernel. The test case simulates a scenario where a parent process writes to a shared range while a child process collapses it, and verifies that the content remains isolated during this process. The patch passes on an unmodified kernel, indicating that the isolation provided by khugepaged collapse is sufficient to prevent data corruption. The new test case is designed to ensure that CoW (Copy-on-Write) functionality works correctly in this scenario.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 12/17] selftests/mm: run every supported collapse order by default
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the selftests/mm/khugepaged test to run every supported collapse order by default, rather than requiring the user to specify a specific order. The test will automatically include all anon THP orders below the PMD context in both the no-argument invocation and the 'all' case. This change also updates the handling of the '-c' option, which now pins one order and reports an error if the specified order is above the PMD or unsupported.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 13/17] selftests/mm: verify synchronous khugepaged driving is attributable
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test to verify that synchronous khugepaged driving is attributable and deterministic. The test uses the huge_memory tracepoints to attribute outcomes and checks that exactly one collapse attempt is made on each prepared window, resulting in the window being collapsed afterwards. The test also sets scan_sleep_millisecs to 60s to prove the wake path. The patch adds a new selftest called khugepaged_sync_check and modifies several files to support it.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 14/17] selftests/mm: add khugepaged race harness
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a selftest harness to exercise the khugepaged functionality under concurrent access scenarios, including faults, GUP pins, fork, mremap, and MADV_DONTNEED operations. The test simulates three different driver modes: stepped (khugepaged running one full pass at a time), free (khugepaged left to run without any intervention), and madvise (MADV_COLLAPSE and MADV_DONTNEED loop). The test ensures that the racing pages are either read as their pattern or as zero, never anything else. The kernel's own assertions are also used to verify the correctness of the test.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 15/17] selftests/mm: race collapse of windows with holes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged_race test to run both ends of the occupancy scale, one after the other, for every driver mode. The test checks for correctness by verifying that every racing page reads as its pattern or zero. The patch also adds a new option -z to narrow a run to the hole-heavy end, and another option -m to narrow it to one mode. This is done to collapse windows with holes, which was not happening before due to the harness pinning max_ptes_none to 0.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 16/17] selftests/mm: add memory-pressure threads to the khugepaged race harness
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two new threads to the khugepaged race harness, which tests the Linux kernel's memory management under various stress conditions. The first thread, 'pageout', simulates swap traffic and LRU churn by repeatedly MADV_PAGEOUTing a dedicated region of memory and checking its contents after each cycle. The second thread, 'compactor', triggers compaction by writing to /proc/sys/vm/compact_memory in a loop, competing with the collapse for pages and refcount elevations. The patch also introduces new command-line options to narrow down the test runs to specific combinations of modes and occupancy limits.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 17/17] selftests/mm: zap whole PTE tables in the khugepaged race harness
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged race harness to occasionally zap a whole PMD-aligned area of pages, rather than just individual pages or tables. This is done to test the empty-table reclaim functionality, which only engages when a zap spans an entire table. The change introduces occasional whole-table zaps every 64 iterations, while maintaining the existing fine-grained page zapping as the common case.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series improves the coverage of selftests for khugepaged, a kernel component that collapses huge pages into smaller ones. The existing tests were incomplete and had issues running on certain environments. This series addresses these problems by scaling the collapse wait time, skipping certain test cases based on PMD size, and adding new test cases to cover more scenarios. New features include folio-order helpers, order-parameterized anon collapse cases, a shared-source write race test, and tests for khugepaged's wake path and synchronization mechanisms.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the collapse_compound_extreme test case failing on arm64 configurations with 512M PMD size due to unreliable allocation of order-13 pages. The author agreed to skip this case where the PMD is larger than 32M, as the MADV_COLLAPSE cases still cover PMD-order collapse on those configurations.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

collapse_compound_extreme builds a PTE table full of distinct PTE-mapped
compound pages by cycling hpage_pmd_nr fault-time THPs through mremap.  It
therefore needs hpage_pmd_nr PMD-order allocations in a row.  That is fine
at a 2M PMD (4K base pages) or a 32M one (16K), but a 512M PMD -- arm64
with 64K base pages -- makes each of those an order-13 allocation, which
the allocator cannot reliably hand out even once, let alone 8192 times.

The failure is not a quiet one: the case calls ksft_exit_fail_msg(), so the
whole binary stops and every case after it is lost.

Skip the case where the PMD is larger than 32M.  The MADV_COLLAPSE cases
still cover PMD-order collapse on those configurations, and 4K and 16K
PMDs are unaffected.

Assisted-by: Claude-Code:claude-opus-5
Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>
---
 tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c | 10 ++++++++++
 1 file changed, 10 insertions(+)

diff --git a/tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c b/tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c
index 9a90ff5f484e..51fc1f04d0a0 100644
--- a/tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c
+++ b/tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c
@@ -1007,6 +1007,16 @@ static void collapse_compound_extreme(struct collapse_context *c, struct mem_ops
 	void *p;
 	int i;
 
+	/*
+	 * The test needs hpage_pmd_nr PMD-order allocations, which is likely to
+	 * fail for large PMD sizes.  Skip if the PMD size is over 32M.
+	 */
+	if (hpage_pmd_size > (32UL << 20)) {
+		ksft_test_result_skip("%s: PMD too large for fault-time THP construction\n",
+				      __func__);
+		return;
+	}
+
 	p = ops->setup_area(1);
 	ksft_print_msg("Construct PTE page table full of different PTE-mapped compound pages\n");
 	for (i = 0; i < hpage_pmd_nr; i++) {
--

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the wait time for khugepaged collapse cases on arm64 with 64K pages, agreeing that three seconds is too thin and proposing to add one second per 128M to the timeout, while keeping three seconds as the floor.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

wait_for_scan() gives every case the same three seconds, whatever the huge
page costs to build.  collapse_full asks for four of them: 8M at a 2M PMD,
but 2G at a 512M PMD -- arm64 with 64K base pages.

Three seconds is thin at that size rather than generous.  Across 80 runs of
collapse_full on arm64 with 64K pages the wait was half a second in 73 of
them, with a tail to two seconds, and the case has timed out in a full
matrix run, reporting a failure for a collapse that was still going.

Keep three seconds as the floor and add a second per 128M to collapse.  A
2M PMD is unchanged.  A 512M PMD gets 19 seconds, which is headroom over
the observed tail rather than a measured requirement.  The budget bounds
how long a real failure takes to report, not how long a passing case
waits: wait_for_scan() returns as soon as the collapse turns up.

arm64/64K: khugepaged all:anon 21 pass/1 fail -> 22 pass/0 fail.  x86-64 is
unchanged.

Assisted-by: Claude-Code:claude-opus-5
Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>
---
 tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c | 4 +++-
 1 file changed, 3 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)

diff --git a/tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c b/tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c
index 51fc1f04d0a0..0f828bfee31f 100644
--- a/tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c
+++ b/tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c
@@ -602,8 +602,10 @@ static bool wait_for_scan(const char *msg, char *p, size_t len,
 		int nr_hpages, int collap_order, struct mem_ops *ops)
 {
 	unsigned long hpage_size = page_size << collap_order;
+	/* Three seconds as a floor, plus a second per 128M to collapse */
+	const unsigned long bytes = (unsigned long)nr_hpages * hpage_size;
+	int timeout = 6 + 2 * (bytes / (128UL << 20));
 	int full_scans;
-	int timeout = 6; /* 3 seconds */
 
 	/* Sanity check */
 	if (!ops->check_huge(p, len, 0, hpage_size))
-- 
2.54.0

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the page cache caps folio order, explaining that it's capped at MAX_PAGECACHE_ORDER on arm64 with 64K base pages, making PMD-sized page cache folios impossible and causing four shmem cases to fail. The author added code to skip these cases when the PMD order has no per-order shmem_enabled control.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

The page cache caps folio order at MAX_PAGECACHE_ORDER, which sits below
the PMD order where a PMD is 512M -- arm64 with 64K base pages.  A
PMD-sized page cache folio is then impossible, so MADV_COLLAPSE answers
-EINVAL and khugepaged passes over the range.  The shmem cases ask for one
anyway, so four of them fail and the run bails out in the middle.

The cap is one global, so it rules out every file mapping, not just shmem:
shmem_huge_global_enabled() drops the PMD order from what it allows, and
file_thp_enabled() refuses a regular file whose mapping cannot hold a PMD
folio.  Skip both mem types when the PMD order has no per-order
shmem_enabled control, which is the readable form of the cap: that control
is created for the orders in THP_ORDERS_ALL_FILE_DEFAULT.  A run left with
nothing to collapse into skips outright.

Anonymous collapse is unaffected: its orders are not capped this way.

Assisted-by: Claude-Code:claude-opus-5
Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>
---
 tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c | 31 +++++++++++++++++++++++++
 1 file changed, 31 insertions(+)

diff --git a/tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c b/tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c
index 0f828bfee31f..9b1da0dd0f8e 100644
--- a/tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c
+++ b/tools/testing/selftests/mm/khugepaged.c
@@ -1424,6 +1424,37 @@ int main(int argc, char **argv)
 
 	setbuf(stdout, NULL);
 
+	/*
+	 * The page cache caps folio order at MAX_PAGECACHE_ORDER, which
+	 * xas_split_alloc() puts below the PMD order on arm64 with 64K pages.
+	 * A PMD-sized page cache folio is then impossible, so the kernel
+	 * refuses these collapses by design and there is nothing to test.
+	 *
+	 * The cap is one global, so it rules out every file mapping, not just
+	 * shmem: shmem_huge_global_enabled() drops the PMD order from what it
+	 * allows, and file_thp_enabled() refuses a regular file whose mapping
+	 * cannot hold a PMD folio.
+	 *
+	 * The per-order shmem_enabled control below is what makes the cap
+	 * readable: it is created for the orders in THP_ORDERS_ALL_FILE_DEFAULT,
+	 * which is the cap and nothing else, so whether the PMD order has one
+	 * answers for a regular file as much as for shmem.
+	 */
+	if (!(thp_shmem_supported_orders() & (1UL << hpage_pmd_order))) {
+		if (shmem_ops) {
+			ksft_print_msg("no PMD-order page cache folio: skipping shmem\n");
+			shmem_ops = NULL;
+		}
+		if (read_only_file_ops) {
+			ksft_print_msg("no PMD-order page cache folio: skipping file\n");
+			read_only_file_ops = NULL;
+			read_write_file_read_ops = NULL;
+			read_write_file_write_ops = NULL;
+		}
+		if (!anon_ops && !shmem_ops && !read_only_file_ops)
+			ksft_exit_skip("Nothing left to collapse into\n");
+	}
+
 	default_settings.khugepaged.max_ptes_none = hpage_pmd_nr - 1;
 	default_settings.khugepaged.max_ptes_swap = hpage_pmd_nr / 8;
 	default_settings.khugepaged.max_ptes_shared = hpage_pmd_nr / 2;
--

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern that the swapout path in khugepaged's collapse mechanism fails to report exact swap counts due to MADV_PAGEOUT being best effort, which can leave folios under writeback from an earlier pageout. The author agreed to restructure the code in v2 to ask again for up to two seconds before reporting failure.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about the lack of functional change in moving the is_backed_by_folio() function to vm_util.c, stating that it's just a code reorganization and no functionality has been altered.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the lack of a function to check if an address range is backed by folios of a specific order, which is necessary for mTHP collapse tests. The author added a new helper function `is_range_backed_by_folio_orders` that checks whether every order-aligned window of the range maps exactly one folio of that order, and explained its implementation.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

An mTHP collapse test has to ask whether a range came out as folios of one
particular order, placed where a collapse would place them.  Nothing
answers that today: is_backed_by_folio() classifies the folio behind a
single page, and check_huge_anon() reads smaps AnonHugePages, which only
accounts PMD mappings.

Add is_range_backed_by_folio_orders().  For every order-aligned window of
the range it requires a present head PFN at its natural alignment and a
contiguous PFN run across the window.  A window stitched together from
several folios, or one holding a folio shifted off its natural position,
fails -- which is what makes the helper usable for "this window collapsed
and that one did not".

Assisted-by: Claude-Code:claude-opus-5
Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>
---
 tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.c | 42 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
 tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.h |  2 ++
 2 files changed, 44 insertions(+)

diff --git a/tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.c b/tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.c
index 3c276865a778..3f586f2c3d33 100644
--- a/tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.c
+++ b/tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.c
@@ -556,6 +556,48 @@ bool is_backed_by_folio(char *vaddr, int order, int pagemap_fd,
 	return false;
 }
 
+/*
+ * Check whether every order-@order window of [start, len) maps exactly one
+ * folio of that order, head to tail.  The address range must be naturally
+ * aligned, each window's PFN run must be contiguous, and a window's first
+ * PFN must be the folio head.
+ *
+ * This is the check "did this range collapse into order-@order folios": a
+ * window assembled from parts of several folios, or mapping a folio shifted
+ * from its natural position, fails.
+ */
+bool is_range_backed_by_folio_orders(char *start, size_t len, int order,
+				     int pagemap_fd, int kpageflags_fd)
+{
+	const unsigned long nr_pages = 1UL << order;
+	const size_t window = nr_pages * psize();
+	char *vaddr;
+
+	if ((uintptr_t)start % window || len % window)
+		return false;
+
+	for (vaddr = start; vaddr < start + len; vaddr += window) {
+		unsigned long pfn = pagemap_get_pfn(pagemap_fd, vaddr);
+		unsigned long i;
+
+		/* Not present, or not mapping the folio head. */
+		if (pfn == -1UL || pfn % nr_pages)
+			return false;
+
+		for (i = 1; i < nr_pages; i++) {
+			if (pagemap_get_pfn(pagemap_fd, vaddr + i * psize()) !=
+			    pfn + i)
+				return false;
+		}
+
+		if (!is_backed_by_folio(vaddr, order, pagemap_fd,
+					kpageflags_fd))
+			return false;
+	}
+
+	return true;
+}
+
 /* If `ioctls' non-NULL, the allowed ioctls will be returned into the var */
 int uffd_register_with_ioctls(int uffd, void *addr, uint64_t len,
 			      bool miss, bool wp, bool minor, uint64_t *ioctls)
diff --git a/tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.h b/tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.h
index 56a28ce7d029..39dfb18dc10c 100644
--- a/tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.h
+++ b/tools/testing/selftests/mm/vm_util.h
@@ -99,6 +99,8 @@ int gather_folio_orders(char *vaddr_start, size_t len,
 		int pagemap_fd, int kpageflags_fd, int orders[], int nr_orders);
 bool is_backed_by_folio(char *vaddr, int order, int pagemap_fd,
 			int kpageflags_fd);
+bool is_range_backed_by_folio_orders(char *start, size_t len, int order,
+				     int pagemap_fd, int kpageflags_fd);
 
 int uffd_register(int uffd, void *addr, uint64_t len,
 		  bool miss, bool wp, bool minor);
--

The author proposed lifting this into khugepaged_full_pass() and driving it through sysfs using a completion barrier for khugepaged.

The test faults memory in with only one order enabled and checks that the helpers classify the backing as exactly that order. A fix is planned.
